sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: steady versus flashing lights, the three arrows, dark and uncontrolled intersections, T intersections, right-of-way and pedestrian-activated signals
Look-alike signal meanings and yield rules from the signal and intersection pages, each tied to one handbook page; hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec09-R01 | anchor: A01
A steady yellow tells you the red is coming, so you stop if you can do so safely before entering, whereas a steady red requires a complete stop and waiting for as long as it stays red. [A01]
Why it matters: group signal lights; difficulty two; confusable sec09-F08 versus sec09-F10.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec09-R02 | anchor: A01
A right turn on a steady red needs a complete stop first and is barred wherever a sign prohibits it. [A01]
Why it matters: group signal lights; difficulty two; prereq sec09-F11.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec09-R03 | anchor: A01
A police officer's directions override what the signal light shows. [A01]
Why it matters: group signal lights; difficulty one; prereq sec09-F03.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec09-R04 | anchor: A02
A flashing red light is treated as a stop sign, while a flashing yellow light only requires slowing down and proceeding with caution. [A02]
Why it matters: group flashing lights; difficulty two; confusable sec09-F13 versus sec09-F14.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec09-R05 | anchor: A02
A red arrow forbids the turn until a green signal appears, while a flashing yellow arrow permits the turn after you yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. [A02]
Why it matters: group arrows; difficulty three; confusable sec09-F15 versus sec09-F18.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec09-R06 | anchor: A02
A yellow arrow is a warning that red is next, and a driver already inside the intersection should finish the turn and clear it rather than stop. [A02]
Why it matters: group arrows; difficulty two; confusable sec09-F16 versus sec09-F17.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec09-R07 | anchor: A02
At a dark signal both vehicles stop, and the tie goes to the driver on the right. [A02]
Why it matters: group intersections; difficulty three; prereq sec09-F21.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec09-R08 | anchor: A02
At a T intersection it is the driver on the street that ends who must yield to traffic on the cross street. [A02]
Why it matters: group intersections; difficulty three; prereq sec09-F22.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec09-R09 | anchor: A03
A dark traffic signal and an intersection with no signals or signs at all are handled the same way, as a 4-way stop. [A03]
Why it matters: group intersections; difficulty two; confusable sec09-F26 versus sec09-F24.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec09-R10 | anchor: A03
On a pedestrian-activated signal, solid red means stop and stay stopped while the pedestrian is in the crosswalk, whereas flashing red means stop and then go once the pedestrian has cleared your half of the road. [A03]
Why it matters: group pedestrian signals; difficulty three; confusable sec09-F35 versus sec09-F36.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec09-R11 | anchor: A03
Flashing yellow on a pedestrian-activated signal means a pedestrian has pressed the button, while solid yellow means prepare to stop. [A03]
Why it matters: group pedestrian signals; difficulty two; prereq sec09-F34.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec09-R12 | anchor: A03
A school crossing stop is required whenever anyone is in the crosswalk, and a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian may never be passed, even on green. [A03]
Why it matters: group pedestrians; difficulty two; confusable sec09-F31 versus sec09-F32.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]
